source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995, Cognitive Science 19) MAC/FAC: A model of similarity-based retrieval - design
finding: MAC/FAC is a two-stage retriever. MAC takes a dot product of cheap content vectors (counts of predicates) and keeps the best item plus anything within a set width. FAC runs the structure matcher SME on the survivors and keeps the best structural matches. The paper sets six criteria a retrieval model must meet: structured representations, structured mappings, primacy of the mundane (most retrievals are literal matches), surface superiority, rare insights (relational remindings occur but less often), and scalability.
numbers: Selector width 10% in the main runs. MAC costs about 0.002 s per pair on 1990s hardware; SME costs 1 to 11 s per pair, about 4 s on average.
limits: A psychological model, not a performance-maximising retriever. By design it returns mostly literal and surface matches and only occasionally pure analogies.
agent_relevance: Our retrieval step can copy the shape: a cheap count-vector pass over many stored cases, then an expensive structure check on a handful. Expect it to return near cases mostly; far analogues will be rare by design.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) - human data: Karla the Hawk reminding study (Gentner, Rattermann & Forbus 1993; Rattermann & Gentner 1987 Exp 2)
finding: People first read 32 stories and, after a delay of about a week, were probed with variants and wrote down any earlier story they were reminded of. Remindings followed literal similarity and surface similarity far more than analogy or first-order-only matches. The order held in three versions of the study.
numbers: 32 stories to remember (20 base, 12 distractors); 20 probes (5 literal, 5 analogy, 5 surface, 5 first-order). Reminding proportions: surface .53, analogy .12, first-order .03; the literal value is garbled in the PDF text (reported as the highest). Order LS >= SF > AN >= FOR across three studies.
limits: Read in this review of the original, not in the 1993 paper itself (the 1993 PDF was a scan with no text layer). Story sets are written by experimenters, so the surface and analogy variants are cleanly separated, unlike real memory.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a retriever tuned to human-like similarity to surface far analogues. If we want far analogues we must add a deliberate relational pass.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) - soundness versus retrievability dissociation
finding: The kinds of match people retrieve are not the kinds they judge sound. Subjects rated analogy and literal matches as significantly more sound than surface and first-order matches, yet surface matches were retrieved about as often as literal ones and analogy matches about a quarter as often.
numbers: Retrieval order LS >= SF > AN >= FOR; soundness order puts AN and LS above SF and FOR. Reported from Gentner et al. 1993 and Rattermann & Gentner 1987.
limits: Second-hand in this paper. Soundness ratings were given for pairs shown side by side, retrieval was from memory.
agent_relevance: Retrieval and verification need separate scores. A retrieval hit rate by surface overlap says nothing about whether the case will transfer.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997, American Psychologist) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity
finding: The review restates the dissociation: the more surface similarity between probe and stored story, the more likely retrieval; the more shared higher-order structure, the higher the rated soundness. Participants often rated their own remindings low in both soundness and similarity. A parallel split appears in problem solving: retrieval follows surface, success follows structure. The review flags a dissenting study (Hammond, Seifert & Gray 1991).
numbers: No new numbers. Cites Holyoak & Koh 1987, Keane 1988, Ross 1987 1989, Seifert et al 1986, Gentner et al 1993.
quote: the kind of similarity that most reliably led to remindings was not the kind participants most valued in making inferences
limits: Review, not a test. The dissenting Hammond et al. study was not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat 'surface-driven retrieval' as the default failure of any similarity memory, human or embedding.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) - Simulation 1: Karla stories, MAC/FAC retrieves the base story
finding: With nine base stories and nine first-order distractors in memory, MAC/FAC retrieved the correct base story for every literal probe, most surface probes and two thirds of analogy probes. The result was identical after MAC and after FAC.
numbers: Proportion correct, MAC and FAC alike: literal 1.0, surface 0.89, analogy 0.67. Memory 18 stories, 27 probes (9 per type).
limits: Far easier than the human task (18 stories against 32 plus life-long memory, no one-week delay). The authors say so. Hand-coded predicate-calculus stories, 9 of 20 story sets.
agent_relevance: Even in a tiny clean memory, pure analogy probes fail one time in three through a count-vector filter. Plan for recall below 100% on far cases.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) - Simulations 2 and 3: what the filter and the structure stage each do
finding: With all four variants of each story in memory and base stories as probes, retrievals ordinally matched the people: literal > surface > analogy > first-order. FAC kept all literal matches MAC passed, kept some partial matches and rejected most unrelated stories. With literal matches removed from memory, surface matches won (SF .88 MAC / .78 FAC, AN .56 / .56, FOR .22 / .11), again the human order.
numbers: MAC output averaged 3.4 items per probe and FAC kept 1.6 (both widths 10%). Other-set stories: 1.33 passed MAC, 0.22 passed FAC (sim 2); 1.11 and 0.11 (sim 3). Memory 36 stories (sim 2), 27 stories (sim 3).
limits: Ordinal fit only; the authors chose ordinal agreement as the criterion. FAC accepts more surface than analogy items only because it is offered a narrow shortlist.
agent_relevance: The structure stage is a precision filter (junk 1.11 -> 0.11) more than a recall booster. Our FAC step should prune, not rescue.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) - comparison with ARCS (Thagard et al. 1990) on the Karla stories
finding: The rival connectionist retriever ARCS, run on the Karla stories among 100 fables, gave activations that break the human order. Surface matches fell below first-order-only matches, and analogy matches fell below first-order matches, so MAC/FAC explained the human data better.
numbers: ARCS asymptotic activations: literal .67, first-order -.11, surface -.17, analogy -.27. Human order: LS >= SF > AN >= FOR.
limits: The comparison was run by the MAC/FAC authors, who say ARCS would not settle on many of their representations (runs up to 12 hours); the authors chose the retrieval cut-off for ARCS themselves. No independent replication was found in this review.
agent_relevance: A cheap count-vector filter can beat a heavier constraint network in both fit and cost. Do not assume the more elaborate retriever is the better one.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) - cost and stability against ARCS (fables, plays)
finding: On the Sour Grapes fable among 100 fables, MAC/FAC returned the right story in 0.2 to 0.3 s and ARCS in 81 to 123 s. When 25 Shakespeare plays were added to memory, ARCS took 251 to 373 s and was pulled to the wrong plays on one probe; MAC/FAC results did not change and took 0.3 to 0.4 s. The authors suggest ARCS may favour larger descriptions.
numbers: ARCS 81-123 s vs MAC/FAC 0.2-0.3 s (125 items: 251-373 s vs 0.3-0.4 s). Memory 100 then 125 items.
limits: 1990s Lisp hardware, tiny memories, hand-encoded corpora. Timings are about scaling shape, not absolute speed.
agent_relevance: Supports the cheap-first design for a memory that grows: the first pass must stay roughly linear and local.

source: Forbus, Gentner & Law (1995) - sensitivity analyses: what the content vector must contain
finding: The model reproduced the human order only in a limited region of selector widths, and only when the content vector counted both attributes and relations. Attribute-only vectors failed. Relation-only vectors worked only in a narrow band (MAC width 40 to 50%, FAC width 20 to 60 or 70%), and there MAC passed so many items that the point of a cheap filter was lost.
numbers: Grid of 11 x 11 selector widths (1 to 100%, steps of 10), 121 runs, about 98,010 MAC executions.
limits: Fits the ordinal pattern, not recall against ground truth. Authors admit width has no theory-given value.
agent_relevance: A first pass built only on relation counts looks tempting but is not enough. Count both relation types and object types, or the shortlist is too big or too wrong.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein, Thompson & Forbus (2009, Cognitive Science 33) Reviving inert knowledge - Exp 1 (management consultants)
finding: Consultants who compared two analogous negotiation cases before recalling a case from their own work retrieved better structural matches than those who studied the cases one at a time. Most recalled cases were analogies, not surface matches, which contradicts the 'surface only' picture for experts recalling freely.
numbers: N = 124 (64 comparison, 60 separate-case). Retrieval rating M 1.25 vs 0.82, t(122) = 2.65, p < .01. Full structural analogy retrieved by 63% (40/64) vs 42% (25/60). Across all: analogy 52%, shallow match 30%, literal 6%, other 11%. Contingent agreements in test negotiation: 59% vs 33%, chi2(1, N = 62) = 4.22. Verified-source retrievals were structural in 68%, unverifiable sources 45%, no source 31%.
limits: Free recall of the person's own past cases, not cue-driven retrieval from a fixed memory; some recalls may be built at recall time (confabulation risk, the reason for Exp 4). 15 years of experience on average, so not novices.
agent_relevance: Retrieval at the moment of use improves if the agent first compares two analogous cases and builds an abstract description of the pair, then searches with that.

source: Gentner et al. (2009) - Exp 2 and 3 replications (students, then wider principle set)
finding: Exp 2 repeated the finding with business students who had little work experience. Exp 3 added a second negotiation principle and a single-case control. The comparison group beat both the separate-case and single-case groups.
numbers: Exp 2: df = 34 (about 36 participants); principle t(34) = 3.41, p < .01; retrieval 1.47 vs 0.59, t(34) = 2.88, p < .01; 95% of comparison vs 18% of separate-case participants linked the two cases. Exp 3: F(1,48) = 8.63, p < .01; Dunnett p < .05 against both controls; 100% vs 36% linked the cases.
limits: Same lab, same task family, same rating scheme; effect sizes not reported as d. Retrieval measured by a coded rating of the recalled case.
agent_relevance: The effect survives a population change; it is not an artifact of expert consultants.

source: Gentner et al. (2009) - Exp 4: controlled memory set, retrieval of a prior analogous story
finding: To rule out recall-time confabulation, participants first read seven negotiation stories, did 30 minutes of unrelated tasks, then saw two analogous probe cases (compared or separately). Comparison raised retrieval of the earlier analogous story and cut retrieval of a surface-similar one.
numbers: N = 73. Analogous story recalled: 27% vs 6%, chi2(1, N = 73) = 6.12, p < .05. Surface-similar story recalled: 30% vs 78%, same test statistic reported.
limits: Absolute analogy recall is low even with the best condition (27%). One 30-minute delay, not days.
agent_relevance: Even a strong intervention leaves most far analogues unretrieved. Design for the 70% that still fail.

source: Gentner et al. (2009) - Exp 5: comparison at test time and problem-solving transfer (Duncker tumor problem, Red Adair)
finding: Comparing two analogous problems at test time raised solution of the tumor problem, but the effect was not reliable for the second problem. Explicit reminding of the earlier analog was rare and similar across groups, yet in the comparison group those who were reminded mostly solved it.
numbers: N = 227. Tumor problem solved 31% vs 5%, chi2(1, N = 227) = 24.71, p < .001. Red Adair 41% vs 30%, p = .08 (ns). Reported being reminded: 18% vs 14%. In comparison condition: 81% solved if reminded (n = 21) vs 33% if not (n = 95); in separate-case 44% (n = 16) vs 31% (n = 95), p = .30.
limits: Second problem shows no reliable effect; authors guess familiarity with fire-fighting. Self-reported reminding is noisy.
agent_relevance: Retrieval is a bottleneck: when it fires, transfer is likely. A reminder rate of 14 to 18% sets the ceiling.

source: Gentner et al. (2009) - Simulations 3 and 4: stored schemas in MAC/FAC
finding: If memory holds abstracted relational schemas, MAC/FAC retrieves them far more often than it retrieves the raw analogous cases. Adding literally similar items to memory crowds out both schemas and analogies.
numbers: Sim 3 (schemas in memory): MAC passed 57% of schemas and 100% of shallow matches; FAC returned 57% schemas, 57% shallow, only 14% of analogical matches. Sim 4 (literal items added): literal items 100% at MAC and FAC; schemas 43% at MAC, 29% at FAC; shallow 14% at FAC; analogies 0%.
limits: Seven story sets, hand-built schemas, simulation not new human data.
agent_relevance: Store abstracted schemas (what was compared and why it fit) next to the raw cases. They are retrieved where the raw far analogue is not.

source: Gentner et al. (2009) - background claims on moderators (expertise, encoding, comparison), as reported in the paper
finding: Failure of relational retrieval is reported to be less severe for experts (Blanchette & Dunbar 2001; Novick 1988). Self-explanation and theme assignment sometimes help but results are inconsistent (Weisberg 1995). Comparison of analogous examples is called the best-established way to promote relational transfer. Two accounts remain open: stored schema abstraction, and learning to encode in a relational way; the authors think encoding is likely part of it.
numbers: No new numbers. Cites Gick & Holyoak 1980 1983, Reeves & Weisberg 1994, Ross 1984 1987 1989, Catrambone 2002, Johnson & Seifert 1992.
limits: Second-hand; the cited studies were not opened here. The schema versus encoding contrast was not settled by these experiments.
agent_relevance: Moderators to test in our agent: how many cases compared, whether an explicit schema is written, and how the case is encoded at storage time.

source: Puranam, Sen & Workiewicz (2025) Can LLMs help improve analogical reasoning for strategic decisions? - human benchmark
finding: A Gick and Holyoak style experiment with two source stories and two business target problems. Humans rarely solved the problem without a hint and a hint helped modestly. Success was below the original 1983 study, which the authors link to the extra matching step.
numbers: Humans n = 199. Factory problem solved 6.3% without hint vs 8.7% (4/46) with hint; HR problem 20.3% vs 37% (17/46). Cited original, Gick & Holyoak 1983 Exp 2: 29% (8/28) without hint vs 50% (14/28) with hint.
limits: Business-school undergraduates; coding of solutions by the authors; the 1983 numbers are as reported by these authors, not checked in the source.
agent_relevance: A hint to use an analogy is a cheap, real lever for people. For the agent the analogue is a programmatic trigger (see G1) rather than a standing instruction.

source: Puranam, Sen & Workiewicz (2025) - GPT-4 versus humans on matching the right source story
finding: GPT-4 almost never used the correct source story without a hint, but with a hint it flagged the correct story every time, along with the wrong one. Humans were the reverse: few false uses, many misses. The authors conclude retrieval-like recall is cheap for the model and matching is the weak step.
numbers: GPT-4 n = 60 runs (15 per cell). No hint: 0 correct matches in both problems (precision, recall, F1 = 0), accuracy 50%. With hint: recall 1.00, precision .50 to .52, F1 .67 to .68, accuracy .50 to .53. Humans with hint: precision .67 to .75, recall .26 to .39, F1 .38 to .51, accuracy .57 to .63. Without hint humans: perfect precision, recall 6.25% (Radiation) and 22% (Dolphin).
limits: Single model, two problems, one prompt style; the authors mention a demand effect (the model says what the hint implies). Preprint.
agent_relevance: A model asked 'is there an analogy?' will say yes to everything. Retrieval hits must be checked by a structure test, not accepted on the model's say-so (G4).

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer & Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives - zero-shot results
finding: Given a query story and two candidates (a system analogy and a distractor), the language models were good when the analogy also shared surface features, and at chance or worse when it did not. GPT-4 scored below random on far analogies. Embedding similarity (SBERT) alone reached 77.9% in the easy setting.
numbers: 1096 triples, 50% chance. Average accuracy over models by case (near analogy vs far distractor, near vs near, far vs far, far analogy vs near distractor): 76.9, 73.2, 45.3, 33.9; overall 57.3. Humans: 98.6, 97.2, 96.8, 91.4; overall 96.0. Far analogies: models 39.6%, humans 94.1%.
limits: Binary forced choice, not search over a large memory. Proverbs supply the high-level message. Models tested include 2023 era models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2, FlanT5).
agent_relevance: Surface-similar distractors are the main danger for any retriever: models drop to about a third accuracy when the wrong candidate looks right.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN - what raised far-analogy performance
finding: Solved demonstrations helped far analogies and hurt near ones. Chain-of-thought demonstrations in which the model first states each story's high-level message helped most on far analogies, and still hurt near ones slightly. Far-analogy demonstrations helped slightly more than near ones.
numbers: GPT-based models gained up to 30 absolute points on far analogies with CoT demonstrations; 2, 4 or 6 demonstrations tested, split evenly between far and near; Llama-2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. Demonstration type experiment run on GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 only.
limits: Gains are on a binary task; not tested as retrieval. Near-analogy loss may come from the model leaning on surface cues.
agent_relevance: Make the model state the abstract message of each case first (abstraction step), then compare messages, rather than compare raw text.

source: Ye, Wang, Andrews & Khashabi (2024) AnaloBench: identification of abstract and long-context analogies - choosing the analogy (T1)
finding: Models came near human level on one-sentence stories but the gap widens with story length, and bigger models help little on long stories. No model beat humans at any length.
numbers: 340 human-written analogies; 15 models (12 open, 3 proprietary). Human accuracy T1: 96.0% (1 sentence), 72.5% (10), 73.3% (30). Gap GPT-4 to humans: 6.9 points at 1 sentence, 28.8 points at 30 sentences. Chance 25%.
limits: Four-way multiple choice; humans checked only T1. Stories are GPT-4 elaborations of one-sentence originals, tested for self-preference bias (little change).
agent_relevance: Long, detail-rich cases bury the relational core. Compress each case to a short abstract before indexing.

source: Ye et al. (2024) AnaloBench - retrieving analogies from a large story bank (T2)
finding: Asked to pick the top analogous stories out of a large bank, long-context GPT-4 and Claude scored near a random-retrieval baseline in most settings. Only GPT-4 Turbo on one-sentence stories was clearly above it.
numbers: Precision-recall for k = 1 to 10; bank sizes with 1, 10 and 30 sentence stories (30-sentence bank about 110K tokens). Human T2 run not done (workload).
limits: Prompted retrieval over the whole bank in context, not an embedding index plus rerank.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on 'put all cases in the prompt and ask which fits'. Use a separate narrowing step.

source: Jung et al. (2026) Cross-Pollination Retrieval - existing retrievers on cross-field transferable ideas
finding: On a new benchmark of papers whose ideas transferred from another field, eleven off-the-shelf retrievers did poorly and retrievers built for science papers did worst on average. An LLM reranker over the same 151 candidates did far better, so the answer is recognisable once in the pool.
numbers: CPR-eval: 1,300 queries, 26 fields, 151 candidates each. Recall@10: best retrievers (Gemini Embedding, inf-retriever-v1-pro) 0.26 vs 0.07 by chance; SPECTER2 0.09; LLM reranker (MiMo-V2.6-Pro) 0.81. Dropping the 50 same-topic candidates: retrievers at most 3.6x random, reranker 8.5x.
limits: Positives are mined from citations, so 'transferable' is the citing author's claim; LLM judges built the labels (agreement with a human annotator is in an appendix, not checked here). Preprint, October 2026.
agent_relevance: This is the filter-then-structure result: a cheap embedding pass misses the far analogue, a structure-aware judge over a shortlist finds it. The cheap pass must still put the target inside the shortlist.

source: Jung et al. (2026) Cross-Pollination Retrieval - fine-tuning, query rewriting, transfer to analogy benchmarks
finding: Contrastive training on 10,573 cross-topic pairs lifted recall a lot, carried over to unseen fields and raised AnaloBench T2 retrieval, while training on web search, citation or reasoning-retrieval data did not. Query rewriting helped but did not close the gap. Without hard negatives most of the AnaloBench gain vanished.
numbers: Recall@10: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B 0.12 -> 0.50; 4B 0.17 -> 0.69; llama-embed-nemotron-8b 0.25 -> 0.70. Other training sets: at most 0.13 (0.6B). HyDE with BM25: 0.16 -> 0.44. Held-out field: +0.21 to +0.36 and +0.38 to +0.54 Recall@10. AnaloBench nDCG@10: +0.04 to +0.12 with CPR-train; the other three training sets lowered it. BRIGHT: up to +0.13. Pools rebuilt with each pooling retriever left out: Recall@10 changed by at most 0.04.
limits: Needs training data and a trained retriever; our scaffold does not train. Same-topic hard negatives are what teach 'structure not topic'.
agent_relevance: If we build a case store, mine hard negatives that share topic but not mechanism. Without them embeddings stay topical.

source: Chen, Chen, Sun & Zhang (2026) Analogical Deep Research - deep-research agents on historical analogies
finding: Commercial and open deep-research agents hardly ever used structural historical analogies when forecasting. They matched on surface features. A pipeline that first decomposes each event into preconditions, timeline, mechanism and outcome, then retrieves on the decomposition, found them.
numbers: ADR-bench, 15 events (10 past, 5 forward). Hidden factors inferred by analogy (HF@L4): all three commercial agents 0/22 on past events and 0/20 on forward ones. MiroFlow plain: at most 1/22. CANA with Sonnet-4.5: 13/22 past, 3/20 forward; with GPT-5.4: 7/22 and 3/20; with Qwen3-8B: 1/22 and 3/20.
limits: 15 events, rubric scored by an LLM judge (Claude Sonnet 4.5), authors built the benchmark and the method; ICML workshop preprint. Theory section is an identifiability argument, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: Retrieve on a mechanism description, not on the situation text. That is a concrete recipe for the cheap first pass of our memory step.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Analogical Deep Research - the gain over self-reflection is small on two of three models
finding: On the analogy-generation benchmark of Li et al., structural decomposition (CANA) beat plain generation by a lot, but the margin over a self-reflection baseline was small for the stronger models.
numbers: Mean MDS score (GPT-5.4 judge): gpt-5.4-mini direct 3.05, self-reflection 3.34, CANA 4.01; sonnet-4-6 direct 2.24, self-reflection 4.11, CANA 4.17; qwen3-8b direct 1.76, self-reflection 3.94, CANA 4.11. Text claims 'more than 10%' over self-reflection.
limits: Computed from the table in the paper; a 10% gain holds for gpt-5.4-mini only (about 20%); for Sonnet it is about 1.5%. LLM judge, single run, no variance reported. This task is generating analogies, not retrieving them.
agent_relevance: Check headline gains per model before trusting them. Most of the benefit may come from any structured rewrite.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR) - self-generated versus retrieved exemplars
finding: Asking the model to recall relevant problems before solving beat zero-shot chain-of-thought on average by about 4%. Against exemplars retrieved by Sentence-BERT from a labelled pool, self-generation won only for strong models; weaker models did better with retrieved exemplars.
numbers: Average gain +4% over baselines across GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench with GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4. At text-davinci-003 on GSM8K, 5-shot retrieved CoT reached 54% against 50% for fixed 5-shot CoT, and self-generated exemplars were higher still (table text partly garbled). K = 3 to 5 exemplars was best; K = 1 underperformed.
limits: No analogy-quality check: the generated 'relevant problems' were judged by outcome only. Retrieval baseline used surface (SBERT) similarity with labelled data. Table 4 partly unreadable in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Self-recall by a strong model is a free baseline to beat. Our retrieval step must out-perform 'ask the model to recall three similar problems' to justify its cost.

source: Liu et al. (2026) HippoSpark - task-level retrieval of experience versus state-level on-demand retrieval
finding: Methods that retrieve whole-task experience before reasoning starts often did no better than, and sometimes worse than, the plain model. Retrieving at the current bottleneck helped. The failure case: two geometry problems looked similar, but one needed combinatorial matching and the other a similar-triangle construction.
numbers: Overall score (mean of AIME24, AIME25, GPQA-Diamond, BigCodeBench-Hard). GPT-5.4-mini: vanilla .326, Trajectory Experience .255, ReasoningBank .306, HippoSpark without experience .409, HippoSpark .483. Qwen3-32B: vanilla .287, ReasoningBank .262, HippoSpark .409. Gains over best baseline +29%, +21%, +28% for three backbones. High-retrieval problems: gains smaller or negative.
limits: Small test sets (AIME is 30 problems per year, 3 to 5 runs); table text is garbled by PDF extraction and was parsed by row order. Authors' own method.
agent_relevance: Task-level similarity is the wrong retrieval key for hard problems. Retrieve at an impasse using the current state (G1), not at start.

source: Xiao et al. (2026) Retrieval-augmented RFT (RA-RFT) - reasoning-aware retriever and the cost of plain retrieval at inference
finding: Training a retriever to rank traces by reasoning usefulness, judged by an LLM on structural rather than surface similarity, improved RL fine-tuning. Prepending the same retriever's top trace at inference to a model never trained with it lowered accuracy.
numbers: Qwen3-1.7B average@32: GRPO 43.3 average over AIME24/25, HMMT25, BrUMO25; GRPO plus inference-time retrieval 37.7; RA-RFT 47.4. AIME25 gain over GRPO +7.1 (1.7B) and +2.8 (4B). Retriever swap: Qwen3-Embedding-4B 38.5 -> 40.5 after gold-relevance fine-tuning, Reason-ModernColBERT 40.7 -> 47.4. Retrieval added to supervised fine-tuning: no benefit (39.7 vs 40.5).
limits: Needs RL training with 64 GPUs; relevance labels from GPT-4o, not verified. Retrieval of traces from a math corpus, not cases for a generalist agent.
agent_relevance: Plain retrieved context can distract. Inject a retrieved case only when the stage calls for it and after the check shows an impasse.

source: Sultan & Shahaf (2023) Life is a circus and we are the clowns - mining analogies between process texts
finding: A sentence-embedding ranking (SBERT) finds paragraph pairs that are textually similar, almost all of them 'self analogies' about the same process. A structural pipeline built on extracted question-answer role pairs finds far, close and sub analogies. Analogies are only 3% of random pairs.
numbers: Top-100 precision: SBERT 100% (mostly self analogies), FMQ 79%, FMV 72%. Mapping accuracy 87% on procedural texts, 94% on psychology stories. Precision@k for FMQ: .84 (25), .77 (50), .79 (75); FMV .68, .72, .71. Expert-judged 100 random pairs: 3% analogies.
limits: Small annotated sets (260 pairs, 15 volunteers); gold labels from one expert; agreement kappa 0.82 binary, 0.58 five-way; relies on QA-SRL extraction.
agent_relevance: Filter ranking by embedding is dominated by same-topic items. Judge 'interesting' by structure, with the base rate in mind (3%).

source: Hope et al. (2022) Scaling creative inspiration with fine-grained functional aspects of ideas - purpose and mechanism retrieval
finding: Retrieving products by extracted purpose and mechanism spans found alternative uses and inspirations better than whole-text embeddings. User studies showed 50 to 60% better results than strong baselines.
numbers: Mean average precision 85 to 87% on alternative-use search vs 40 to 60% for baselines. About 62% of inspirations rated useful; BERT-based variant 51% while the best baseline stayed under 30%. Span extraction F1 about 48% (graph network).
limits: Crowd-worker evaluations on product descriptions; extraction is noisy; effect depends on the quality of the purpose and mechanism spans.
agent_relevance: A short 'purpose + mechanism' summary of each case, used as the index key, is a tested way to retrieve across surface differences.
